Claude Code is built for developers who want an agent that can carry a full, multi-step task from plan to completion, not just help edit a file. It’s especially strong when the job spans several files, migrations, and tests, because it’s designed to read the repo, make targeted changes, run commands, and report back with clear outcomes.

Compared with opencode’s lightweight terminal workflow, Claude Code adds more process scaffolding: plan mode, reusable “skills” for disciplined routines, sub-agents for parallel work, and memory features that help keep longer efforts coherent. results.title: /dev for Claude Code: Claude Code as a Tech Lead with parallel Worker Agents | Product Hunt
results.content:
> 2. Conflicts with your existing superpowers skills. You already have superpowers:brainstorming, superpowers:executing-plans, superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents, superpowers:using-git-worktrees, and superpowers:requesting-code-review — which cover the same ground but in a modular, pick-what-you-need way. This skill would be a monolithic replacement that's less flexible.
> 3. Rigid "never write code in main conversation" rule. The skill's core constraint is that all code must go through worker agents and PRs. That's overkill when you want me to just tweak a SwiftUI view or fix a layout issue. [...] > 4. Low community signal. 10 stars, 0 forks, 7 commits, single contributor. The skill files themselves are well-structured and I didn't find anything malicious — the install script just copies markdown files — but it's very early-stage.
>
> Bottom line: Your current skill setup already gives you subagent orchestration, worktree isolation, and code review when you want them, without forcing every change through a heavyweight process. This skill would slow you down more than it helps. [...] During coding — each Worker runs in an isolated git worktree, does a 6-category counterexample self-check (null, boundary, concurrency, malicious input…), and checks for file-overlap conflicts with other open Issues.

Before merging — mandatory security audits (bandit/npm audit), structured code review with veto conditions (e.g., any direct DDL = auto-reject), and post-merge PR coordination.

Think of it as: Claude Code gives you the agents, /dev gives you the SOP that keeps them from shipping broken code. It's the difference between "write code in parallel" and "run a disciplined engineering team."
